units.title: Affine maps, nonlinearities and logits
outcomes: Write the batched affine map \(Y = XW + 1 b^\top\) with exact shapes, and derive its weight, bias and input gradients.
Derive ReLU, sigmoid and tanh derivatives from their definitions, and state where each saturates or dies.
Explain why stacked affine maps without a nonlinearity collapse to one affine map, and what logits are.
units.why: Every network is affine maps plus nonlinearities, and the raw affine outputs (logits) feed every loss in this section. Wrong shapes or a dead activation here break everything downstream.

next.note: Feed logits into a stable softmax and cross-entropy.
Differentiate affine chains with the chain rule.

study.title: Shallow and deep affine structure
study.locator: Chapter 3, Sections 3.1 to 3.5 (Eq 3.1 to 3.12, printed pp. 25 to 35) for the scalar, multivariate and general affine-plus-activation forms; Chapter 4, Sections 4.1 to 4.4 (Eq 4.1 to 4.16, printed pp. 41 to 49) for composed maps and matrix notation

study.title: MLP math and activation curves
study.locator: Hidden Layers: the linear-collapse derivation \(W = W_1 W_2\), \(b = b_1 W_2 + b_2\) with \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\), \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times h}\); Activation Functions: ReLU, sigmoid and tanh definitions, plots and derivative maxima
study.depth: Skip the Universal Approximators discussion and the Exercises until practice. For the convention that this book calls affine maps linear, read the Chapter 3 Notes paragraph "Linear, affine, and nonlinear functions" in UDL (p. 39).

focus: Batched affine: \(X\) \((n \times d)\), \(W\) \((d \times h)\), \(b\) \((h,)\) broadcasts over rows, so \(Y = XW + 1 b^\top\) has shape \((n, h)\). The bias gradient is the row sum of the upstream gradient.

Without a nonlinearity, two affine layers collapse to one: substituting \(H = XW_1 + b_1\) into \(O = HW_2 + b_2\) gives \(W = W_1 W_2\) and \(b = b_1 W_2 + b_2\). Depth without activation adds no function class.
Sigmoid slope peaks at 0.25 at input 0; tanh peaks at 1 at input 0; both decay toward 0 for large \(|x|\). ReLU has slope 0 below 0 and 1 above; D2L takes the left derivative, 0, exactly at 0.

GELU is \(x\) times the standard Gaussian CDF, smooth rather than piecewise linear, with \(\operatorname{GELU}(0) = 0\) and slope 0.5 at 0. UDL Figure 3.13 (p. 37) names it Gaussian error linear unit.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, for \(X\) \((4 \times 3)\), \(W\) \((3 \times 5)\), \(b\) (5,) and upstream \(G = dL/dY\): write \(Y\) shape \((4 \times 5)\) and derive \(dL/dW = X^\top G\), \(dL/db\) = sum of \(G\) over rows, \(dL/dX = G W^\top\). Then derive the sigmoid, tanh and ReLU derivatives and state each maximum.
traps: Returning \(G\) itself, or its mean, as the bias gradient. The bias is broadcast over the \(n\) rows, so \(dL/db = 1^\top G\), the sum over the batch with shape \((h,)\). A mean belongs only to an explicit mean in the loss.
Reading ReLU slope at 0 as mathematically settled. Frameworks pick a subgradient (D2L uses 0); the kink matters for gradient checks in a later unit.
Assuming tanh fixes the sigmoid saturation problem. It is zero-centered but still saturates, and its per-layer factor is at most 1.

selfTest.q: \(X\) is \((4 \times 3)\), \(W\) is \((3 \times 5)\), \(b\) has 5 entries. What is the shape of \(Y = XW + b\), and of \(dL/dW\) in terms of \(G = dL/dY\)?
selfTest.a: \(Y\) is \((4 \times 5)\). \(dL/dW = X^\top G\) is \((3 \times 4)\) times \((4 \times 5)\) = \(3 \times 5\). \(dL/db\) is the sum of \(G\) over the 4 rows.

selfTest.q: Why do two stacked affine layers without an activation collapse?
selfTest.a: Substitution gives a single affine map with \(W = W_1 W_2\) and \(b = b_1 W_2 + b_2\), so the pair expresses nothing a single layer cannot.

selfTest.q: What are the maximum slopes of the sigmoid and tanh, and where?
selfTest.a: Sigmoid peaks at 0.25 at input 0; tanh peaks at 1 at input 0. Both approach 0 for large positive or negative inputs.

selfTest.q: What are GELU(0) and the GELU slope at 0?
selfTest.a: \(\operatorname{GELU}(0) = 0\) since 0 times \(\Phi(0)\) is 0. The derivative is \(\Phi(x) + x \phi(x)\), so at 0 it equals \(\Phi(0) = 0.5\).

study.title: The max-subtraction trick
study.locator: Softmax classifier: \(L_i = -f_{y_i} + \log \sum_j e^{f_j}\); Practical issues: Numeric stability: the f -= np.max(f) code turning [123, 456, 789] into [-666, -333, 0]

study.title: Masked reductions in cross_entropy
study.locator: ignore_index and reduction parameters: ignored targets contribute no gradient, and mean averages over the non-ignored targets only

focus: Max subtraction is exact, not approximate: shifting every logit by \(c\) multiplies numerator and denominator by \(e^c\), which cancels. The largest shifted logit is 0, so every \(\exp\) input is at most 0 and no term overflows.

The fused per-example loss is \(L_i = -f_{y_i} + \log \sum_j \exp(f_j)\), and its logit gradient is \(\operatorname{softmax}(z)\) minus one-hot(\(y\)). This matches centered differences to about 1e-9 in float64.

Binary cross-entropy with logits must use the log-sigmoid form, never sigmoid followed by log: a confident sigmoid rounds to exactly 0 or 1 and the log is then infinite. Its logit gradient is \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(z) - y\).
Mean divides every gradient by \(N\); a masked mean divides by the valid count and gives masked positions exactly zero gradient. D2L cross_entropy uses reduce_mean; UDL least squares (Eq 5.11) sums.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement log_softmax with max subtraction and a cross-entropy returning per-example losses plus their mean. Derive \(dL/dz = \operatorname{softmax}(z)\) minus one-hot(\(y\)). Show softmax([1000, 1001, 1002]) = [0.0900, 0.2447, 0.6652], and explain why the naive form returns [nan, nan, nan].
traps: Taking \(\log(\operatorname{softmax}(z))\) in two steps. Even with max subtraction, a very small probability can underflow to 0 and its log becomes -inf. log_softmax(z) = \((z - m) - \log \sum \exp(z - m)\), with \(m\) the max, never forms the probability.
Clipping probabilities after a naive softmax to fix overflow. exp(1000) already overflowed to inf and the division already produced nan; clipping cannot recover the true distribution.
Expecting the stable answer on [1000, 1001, 1002] to be [1, 0, 0]. Only logit gaps matter, so the result equals softmax([0, 1, 2]): about [0.09, 0.245, 0.665].

selfTest.q: Why does subtracting the maximum logit prevent overflow without changing softmax?
selfTest.a: Softmax depends only on logit differences: shifting all logits by \(c\) scales numerator and denominator by the same \(e^c\). After subtracting the max, the largest \(\exp\) input is 0, so every term is at most 1.

selfTest.q: What is the gradient of the per-example cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
selfTest.a: \(\operatorname{softmax}(z)\) minus one-hot(\(y\)): \(p_k - 1\) at the true class, \(p_j\) elsewhere. It matches centered finite differences to about 1e-9 in float64.

selfTest.q: A batch of 5 has 2 masked positions under a masked mean. What is the divisor, and what gradient do masked positions get?
selfTest.a: The divisor is the valid count, 3. Masked positions get exactly zero gradient, matching ignore_index semantics.

selfTest.q: Why must binary cross-entropy with logits avoid sigmoid-then-log?
selfTest.a: A confident logit makes sigmoid round to exactly 0 or 1 in floating point, and \(\log(0)\) is infinite. The fused log-sigmoid form stays finite, with gradient \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(z) - y\).

Implement a scalar autodiff engine with topological backward that matches centered finite differences.
Explain vector-Jacobian products: the reverse pass multiplies each incoming gradient by the local Jacobian, seeded with 1 for a scalar loss.
units.why: Frameworks hide this loop, but every gradient bug in later sections is a broken graph, a wrong local derivative or a missed accumulation. The engine you build here is the reference for all of them.

study.title: Backprop equations and graph cost

study.depth: The worked model omits biases by statement; Exercise 2 asks you to add one. Do not mistake the \(W\)-only equations for a complete MLP.

study.title: The vector-Jacobian seed
study.locator: Opening paragraphs on the computational graph and backpropagation; Section 2.5.2 Backward for Non-Scalar Variables: y.backward(gradient=torch.ones(len(y))) computing \(v^\top \partial y / \partial x\)

focus: Forward pass saves what backward needs: UDL Observation 1 stores every hidden activation because weight gradients are computed from them (\(dL/dW_2\) needs \(h\)). Saving is a design obligation, not caching.

Reverse accumulation visits nodes in reverse topological order and multiplies the incoming gradient by each local derivative. That product is the vector-Jacobian product; a scalar loss seeds it with 1.
PyTorch backward on a non-scalar needs the seed vector explicitly (the gradient argument), while MXNet and TensorFlow sum first. A missing seed is an error, not an implicit sum, in PyTorch.
Training memory exceeds prediction memory because intermediates are retained for backward, scaling with layers times batch (D2L). Prediction keeps only the current layer.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the UDL toy forward (Eq 7.9) for one example, derive \(dL/df_3 = 2(f_3 - y)\) down through the chain to the \(w_0\) term, then implement scalar Value objects with topological backward and match centered differences on the neuron graph.
traps: Running backward in forward order. A node must accumulate every downstream contribution before propagating further; forward order uses unfinished gradients.
Assuming saved activations are optional. Without the forward values, local derivatives at nonlinearities and the outer products for weights cannot be evaluated.
Calling backward twice on the same graph to get the same gradient. The second call re-accumulates (a later unit shows why); kept graphs also keep their saved memory alive.

selfTest.q: Why does the forward pass store every hidden activation?
selfTest.a: Backward evaluates local derivatives at the forward values: weight gradients need \(h\) (\(dL/dW_2\) uses \(h^\top\)) and nonlinearity derivatives need their inputs. Without them the chain rule has no numbers.

selfTest.q: A node feeds two downstream ops. What is its reverse-mode gradient?
selfTest.a: The sum of the vector-Jacobian products over both outgoing edges, by the multivariate chain rule. Accumulation is covered fully in the next unit.

selfTest.q: In PyTorch, what does y.backward() do when y = x * x is a vector?
selfTest.a: It raises an error. PyTorch needs an explicit seed vector, as in y.backward(gradient=torch.ones(len(y))), which computes \(v^\top \partial y / \partial x\).

selfTest.q: For loss \((f_3 - y)^2\), what is \(dL/df_3\)?
selfTest.a: \(2(f_3 - y)\) (UDL Eq 7.11). It seeds the whole reverse chain.

selfTest.q: When is forward-mode differentiation cheaper than reverse mode?
selfTest.a: Roughly when there are fewer inputs than outputs: forward mode costs about one pass per input dimension, reverse mode about one pass per output. A scalar loss with many parameters favors reverse mode.

study.title: Exact broadcast contract
study.locator: General semantics: trailing-dimension rules, prepend-1 alignment, result size as the per-dimension max, with (5, 1, 4, 1) plus (3, 1, 1) giving (5, 3, 4, 1); In-place semantics: an in-place tensor may not change shape

study.title: Saved forward values
study.locator: Chapter 7, Section 7.2 Observation 1 (printed pp. 97 to 98): run the network and store the activations of all hidden units in the forward pass for later gradient computation

focus: A node feeding two downstream ops gets the sum of both vector-Jacobian products. PyTorch .grad also accumulates across backward calls, so a missing zero_() silently adds yesterday's gradient to today's.

Broadcast forward: align trailing dimensions, prepend 1 to the shorter shape, and take the per-dimension max. Backward inverts it: sum the upstream gradient over exactly the axes where the input had size 1 or a prepended dimension, then reshape back.

For \(L = \sum((X + b)^2)\) with \(X\) (2, 3) and \(b\) (3,): \(dL/dX = 2(X + b)\) keeps shape (2, 3), while \(dL/db\) = 2 times the sum of \((X + b)\) over rows. This matches centered differences to about 1e-8 in float64.

Leaves are user-created tensors with requires_grad; intermediates carry the graph. Backward saves the forward values its local derivatives need (activations for weights, inputs for nonlinearities); detaching cuts provenance so gradients stop at the cut.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, for \(L = \sum((X + b)^2)\) with \(X\) (2, 3) and \(b\) (3,): derive \(dL/db\) as 2 times the row sums of \((X + b)\) and \(dL/dX\) as \(2(X + b)\). Implement broadcast plus accumulation in your blank-file engine and match centered differences.
traps: Averaging instead of summing at a branch. The \(1/N\) factor belongs to an explicit mean op, never to fan-out: a doubly used node contributes twice.
Summing over the wrong axes in unbroadcast. Sum exactly the axes where the input was size 1 or prepended; summing a full-size axis silently shrinks a real dimension.
Assuming backward zeroes .grad. It adds; the D2L page states this explicitly for PyTorch, unlike MXNet and TensorFlow which reset.

selfTest.q: z = x * u with u = y.detach() and y = x * x. What is \(dz/dx\), and why not \(3x^2\)?
selfTest.a: \(u\). Detach wipes provenance, so \(x\) influences \(z\) only directly through the \(x\) factor; the path through \(y\) carries no gradient. D2L verifies x.grad == u.

selfTest.q: What is the shape of (5, 1, 4, 1) plus (3, 1, 1), and over which axes is the smaller operand's gradient summed?
selfTest.a: The result is (5, 3, 4, 1). The smaller operand aligns as (1, 3, 1, 1), so its gradient sums over dims 0 and 2, then reshapes to (3, 1, 1).

selfTest.q: What happens on a second backward call without zero_()?
selfTest.a: The new gradient adds to the stored one. That suits optimizing a sum of objectives but corrupts per-batch training.

selfTest.q: For \(y = XW + b\) inside a deeper network, which values must backward have available?
selfTest.a: \(X\), for \(dL/dW = X^\top G\), and \(W\), for \(dL/dX = G W^\top\). \(W\) costs no extra memory because the parameter is alive anyway; \(X\) is the activation memory backward forces you to keep. \(dL/db\) needs only \(G\).

study.title: The gradient-check protocol
study.locator: Gradient Checks: the centered formula with \(O(h^2)\) error, relative error with the 1e-2 / 1e-4 / 1e-7 bands, double precision, \(h\) near 1e-5, kinks at ReLU, few datapoints, burn-in point, regularization and dropout discipline, and checking a few dimensions per parameter

study.title: Where the formula comes from
study.locator: The limit definition of the derivative and the linear approximation \(f(x + \epsilon) \approx f(x) + \epsilon f'(x)\): finite differences evaluate the quotient at small nonzero \(\epsilon\) instead of taking the limit
study.depth: Read for the definition only. The centered formula, error orders and protocol all come from the CS231n note above.

study.title: Framework defaults and the overlap warning
study.locator: Signature defaults eps 1e-6, atol 1e-5, rtol 1e-3; the note that checked tensors with overlapping memory, for example expand outputs, will likely fail

focus: Use the centered form \((f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h\). On \(\exp\) at 1 with \(h = 10^{-5}\) it errs by about 6e-11 (second order), while one-sided errs by about 1.4e-5 (first order).

Compare with relative error \(|a - n| / \max(|a|, |n|)\) and pass both-zero explicitly. CS231n bands: above 1e-2 probably wrong, 1e-4 to 1e-2 uncomfortable, below 1e-4 fine with kinks, 1e-7 or less happy.
Run in float64: centered differences on \(\exp\) at 1 err by about 1e-2 in float32 against about 6e-11 in float64. Smaller \(h\) is not always better; roundoff grows as truncation shrinks.

ReLU at exactly 0 gives centered 0.5 against analytic 0, a relative error of 1: the signature of a crossed kink, not a broken derivative. Check few datapoints, past burn-in, with regularization off and noise seeded or disabled.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, implement gradcheck(f, x) with centered differences in float64, \(h = 10^{-5}\) and relative error. Show \(\exp\) matching to below 1e-7, and ReLU at 0 giving 0.5 against analytic 0.
traps: Using absolute error on tiny gradients. A 1e-4 gap on 1e-5 gradients is a huge failure; relative error exists for exactly this case.
Checking with regularization on or dropout active. The simple regularization gradient then dominates or noise swamps the comparison, masking a wrong data-loss gradient.
Perturbing one element of expanded or otherwise overlapping memory. Every aliased index moves at once, so the numerical gradient is meaningless and the check fails on correct code.

selfTest.q: One-sided differences on \(\exp\) at 1 with \(h = 10^{-5}\) err by about 1.4e-5. What does centered achieve, and why?
selfTest.a: About 6e-11. Taylor expansion cancels the first-order term, leaving \(O(h^2)\) error instead of \(O(h)\).

selfTest.q: Analytic gradient is 0 and numerical is 0.5 at a ReLU evaluated at 0. What is the relative error, and what does it mean?
selfTest.a: \(|0 - 0.5| / \max(0, 0.5) = 1\). The perturbations crossed the kink, so the centered quotient averages both sides; it indicts the check point, not the implementation.

selfTest.q: Both analytic and numerical gradients are exactly 0. Pass or fail?
selfTest.a: Pass, by an explicit both-zero rule. The ratio form would divide zero by zero.

selfTest.q: A correct gradient shows relative error near 1e-2 in float32. What do you change?
selfTest.a: Rerun the check in float64. Single-precision roundoff alone can fail a correct gradient; the same \(\exp\) check drops to about 6e-11 in float64.

selfTest.q: Why does torch gradcheck warn about expand outputs as inputs?
selfTest.a: Expanded indices share memory, so perturbing one index changes all its aliases at once. Point perturbation assumes independent coordinates.

units.title: Tensor layout: shape, stride, views and copies
outcomes: Compute an element address from shape, stride and index, and predict contiguity after transpose or slicing.
Classify each reshape, transpose, slice and index operation as view or copy, and state the reshape and indexing rules you may not rely on.
Handle noncontiguous inputs in your own engine: read them correctly through strides or copy to contiguous first, and justify the choice.
units.why: A tensor is storage plus an interpretation. Backward passes that assume contiguous input misread transposed data, and view-versus-copy mistakes turn a reshape into silent corruption.

next.note: See what views plus mutation do to gradients.
Meet storage, strides and views in the framework.

study.title: Tensor creation, shape and memory reuse
study.locator: Getting Started: arange, zeros, ones, shape, size and reshape with -1 inference; Indexing and Slicing; Saving Memory: Y = Y + X reallocates (id changes) while Z[:] = X + Y and X += Y reuse storage
study.depth: The page never defines stride, view or storage: those come from the two PyTorch notes below. Use this page for construction, shape inference and the realloc-versus-reuse demos.

study.title: Which ops share storage
study.locator: The view/storage sharing example with data_ptr and mutation through the view; the transpose example turning a contiguous tensor non-contiguous with no data movement; the full view-ops list; reshape may-copy and contiguous conditional-copy notes; basic indexing returns views while advanced indexing copies

study.title: Strides as element steps
study.locator: Stride definition: per-dimension element steps that, with storage_offset, locate every element; combine with the Tensor Views transpose and expand layouts

focus: A tensor is storage plus shape, stride, offset and dtype. Element [2, 1] of a (3, 4) C-contiguous float32 tensor sits at offset \(2 \times 4 + 1 \times 1 = 9\), so the strides are (4, 1) in elements. NumPy reports the same layout in bytes: (16, 4) for float32.

Transpose swaps shape and strides without moving data: (3, 4) with strides (4, 1) becomes (4, 3) with strides (1, 4), non-contiguous but still a view, so [1, 2] of the transpose aliases offset 9 of the base.

Reshape, reshape_as and flatten may return a view or a copy: never rely on which. view() demands a compatible layout instead. Basic indexing gives views; advanced indexing (integer or boolean arrays) copies.
Expand is a stride-0 view: no storage advances along the stretched axis, which is why perturbing one expanded element moves all its aliases and breaks point-wise gradient checks.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, for a C-contiguous (3, 4) float32 tensor: give strides (4, 1) and offset 9 for [2, 1]; after transpose give shape (4, 3), strides (1, 4), non-contiguous, with [1, 2] aliasing offset 9. Then classify view, reshape, transpose, x[0] and x[[0, 2]] as copy or view.
traps: Assuming transpose or reshape copies. Both can be views: writing through them mutates the base, and the docs mutate t through b to prove it.
Assuming view() always works. It needs a compatible layout; a transposed tensor needs reshape (which may copy) or .contiguous() first.
Mixing byte and element strides. Torch strides count elements; NumPy .strides counts bytes. Convert with itemsize before comparing.

selfTest.q: A (3, 4) float32 tensor is C-contiguous. What are its strides, and what is the offset of [2, 1]?
selfTest.a: Strides (4, 1) in elements. Offset \(2 \times 4 + 1 \times 1 = 9\).

selfTest.q: Transpose it. What are the new shape, strides and contiguity, and which base offset does [1, 2] read?
selfTest.a: Shape (4, 3), strides (1, 4), non-contiguous view. Offset \(1 \times 1 + 2 \times 4 = 9\), the same element.

selfTest.q: Which of these copy: x[0], x[[0, 2]], x.reshape(-1), x.transpose(0, 1)?
selfTest.a: Only x[[0, 2]] is guaranteed to copy (advanced indexing). x[0] and the transpose are views; reshape may be either, so code must not rely on it.

selfTest.q: Y = Y + X versus Y[:] = X + Y: which reallocates, and how do you tell?
selfTest.a: The first reallocates: id(Y) changes. The second reuses storage. D2L demonstrates both with id().

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: noncontiguous and transposed inputs to your engine, view-versus-copy storage checks with shared-storage assertions, and offset accounting verified against the framework on adversarial shapes.
units.stopWhen: You compute strides, offsets and aliasing for transpose and expand cases from memory, and your engine reads a transposed input correctly either through strides or through an explicit contiguous copy.

fit.note: Coverage failed for stride, view, storage and noncontiguous layouts: D2L never mentions them, so the PyTorch Tensor Views and stride references supply the contract, with integrated practice assigned to the mini-project.

units.title: Aliasing, mutation and module ownership
outcomes: Predict when an in-place or view mutation corrupts backward, and route around it with out-of-place ops or no-grad updates.
Explain detach as a provenance cut, and diagnose detached-path and forgotten-zeroing gradient bugs from their signatures.
State module ownership at mechanism level: recursive parameter collection, parameters versus buffers, and who may mutate what.
units.why: Views alias memory, in-place ops rewrite history, and detach cuts the graph without warning. Ownership rules decide which tensor the optimizer may touch and which state merely travels along.

next.note: Meet parameters, buffers and init in the framework.
See views, leaves and in-place ops in autograd state.

study.title: In-place hazards and the version counter
study.locator: In-place operations with autograd: in-place is discouraged because it rewrites the graph instead of allocating new nodes; In-place correctness checks: every tensor keeps a version counter, and accessing a saved tensor whose version changed raises an error

study.title: Detach and the training loop contract
study.locator: Section 2.5.3 Detaching Computation: u = y.detach() with z = u * x gives gradient \(u\), not \(3x^2\), while the graph to y persists; Section 2.5.1: the gradient buffer accumulates, so x.grad.zero_() resets it between objectives

study.title: Parameters versus buffers
study.locator: Parameters and buffers documentation: modules collect parameters recursively for the optimizer; register_buffer holds persistent non-parameter tensors that are saved alongside parameters without getting gradients

focus: Every tensor carries a version counter, bumped by each in-place op. Backward saved the counter value too, so mutating a needed value raises an error instead of computing a wrong gradient. Treat the error as a correct alarm, not an obstacle.
In-place graph rewrites are only safe for updates outside tracking: optimizer steps mutate parameters under no-grad. Anything inside the tracked graph should allocate new nodes.

Detach cuts provenance silently: gradients stop at the cut and read as correct-looking smaller values (\(u\) instead of \(3x^2\)). A forgotten zero_() is the mirror bug: values look plausible but sum two objectives.

Ownership: a module owns its parameters recursively (TensorTonic parameter collection below), the optimizer mutates exactly those, and buffers carry persistent non-differentiated state such as running statistics.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two canonical failures. First, h = x.sigmoid() saves its output; mutate h in place with h.mul_(2) before backward and read the version-counter error. Second, with y = x * x and u = y.detach(), show that z = x * u gives \(dz/dx = u = x^2\), not \(3x^2\). Then state the parameter-versus-buffer rule for a layer with a running counter.
traps: Silencing the version-counter error by mutating through .data. Changes made through .data skip the version counter, so backward runs without an error on the mutated value and returns a wrong gradient. Fix the order of operations or clone before the mutation instead.

Detaching a hidden activation on the path to the loss. Everything before the cut gets no gradient (.grad stays None) with no error, while later layers still train. Detaching the loss itself does fail loudly; the silent case is the middle of the network.
Registering persistent state as a Parameter. It then gets gradients and optimizer updates it should never have; buffers travel in state without differentiation.

selfTest.q: You modify a saved activation in place, then call backward. What happens?
selfTest.a: PyTorch raises a version-counter error when backward accesses the modified saved tensor. The counter recorded at save time no longer matches.

selfTest.q: For z = x * u with u = y.detach() and y = x * x, what is \(dz/dx\)?
selfTest.a: \(u\), i.e. \(x^2\) in value. Provenance through \(y\) is cut, so the \(2x^2\) path contributes nothing and the total is not \(3x^2\).

selfTest.q: Two backward calls with no zero_(): what is in .grad, and when is that what you want?
selfTest.a: The sum of both gradients. Wanted when optimizing a sum of objectives; a bug when the calls were meant to be separate batch updates.

selfTest.q: A layer keeps a running event counter alongside its weights. Parameter or buffer?
selfTest.a: Buffer. It must persist and save with the module but never receive gradients or optimizer updates.
